title: Psalm 133: How Good and Pleasant When Brothers Dwell Together
summary: The psalm celebrates the goodness of brothers living together in unity, and it compares that unity to fine oil poured on Aaron's head, running down his beard to his robes, and to the dew of Mount Hermon falling on the mountains of Zion. There, it says, the LORD has commanded his blessing: life forevermore.
story: Psalm 132 celebrated God's choice of Zion and his promise to David. Psalm 133 describes what happens when God's people gather there in harmony. It is the second-to-last of the Songs of Ascents, and it is the only one devoted entirely to the relationships among God's people. After psalms about the road, the city, the nation's sufferings, God's forgiveness, and God's promises, the collection pauses to celebrate the unity that worship creates. Psalm 134, the final Song of Ascents, will close the collection with a blessing from the temple at night.
historical:
The heading reads “A song of ascents. Of David.” As with other psalms in the collection, the Hebrew phrase can mean by, for, or about David, and scholars differ on how to read it. Those who connect it with David point to the reunification of Israel's tribes under his rule after years of division following Saul's death (2 Samuel 5:1-3), when the tribes came to David at Hebron and said they were his own flesh and blood. Others read it as a later psalm sung by pilgrims from different regions gathered in Jerusalem for the festivals, or after the exile, when the scattered people of Israel were being regathered.

The phrase “brothers live together” also appears in Deuteronomy 25:5, which describes brothers dwelling together on the family land. Some interpreters think the psalm first celebrated the ideal of an extended family keeping its inheritance undivided rather than splitting it among heirs. In the context of the Songs of Ascents, it came to describe the whole people of God gathered at Zion.
cultural:
Oil was used in Israel for food, light, medicine, and anointing. Pouring oil on the head was a sign of honor and welcome to a guest (Psalm 23:5; Luke 7:46), and it was also how priests and kings were consecrated. The oil in verse 2 is specifically the oil of Aaron's anointing as high priest (Exodus 29:7; Leviticus 8:12), a special mixture of olive oil and spices that was reserved for holy use (Exodus 30:22-33). Poured generously, it ran down from his head through his beard to the collar of his robes, marking the whole priest as set apart for God.

Mount Hermon is the highest mountain in the region, rising over 9,000 feet at the northern edge of Israel's territory, and its heights are often covered in snow. It is known for heavy dew, which was vital for crops in the dry months when no rain falls. Zion is far to the south. Some interpreters take the image literally, as moisture carried south from Hermon; most read it poetically: the lush dew of the north falling on the dry hills of Jerusalem, as surprising and refreshing as unity among a divided people.
literary: Psalm 133 is a short wisdom psalm with a single theme. It begins with an exclamation of delight in the goodness of unity, then develops it through two similes. Both images describe something that comes down: the oil runs down from Aaron's head, and the dew falls on Zion's mountains. The Hebrew verb for going down (yarad) appears three times, tying the images together. Blessing flows from above, from God, and it flows generously. The final verse names the source: “there the LORD has bestowed the blessing of life forevermore.” The psalm moves from a human relationship to a priestly anointing to the natural world to God's gift of life, all connected by the image of abundance falling from above.

outline.t: How good and pleasant is unity
Like oil on Aaron's head, running down
Like the dew of Hermon on Zion; the blessing of life

doctrines.note: Unity among God's people is described as good, pleasant, and a place where God commands his blessing. The psalm sees harmony among brothers not as a human achievement but as something that comes down from God, like oil and dew.
The image of Aaron's anointing connects unity with consecration. The whole priest was covered by the oil; so God's blessing covers his gathered people and sets them apart for him.

words.note: Yachad, together or in unity. It describes things joined or happening at the same time, and here it describes brothers living in harmony. The word later gave its name to the community at Qumran, known from the Dead Sea Scrolls, who called themselves the Yachad.

Yarad, to go down or descend. It appears three times in the psalm, describing the oil running down Aaron's head and beard and the dew falling on Zion. The repetition emphasizes that the blessing of unity comes from above.

Tal, dew. In a land with a long dry season, dew was vital for crops, and it became a symbol of God's refreshing blessing (Genesis 27:28; Hosea 14:5). The dew of Hermon was proverbially heavy, and the psalm imagines it falling on Zion as a picture of abundant life.

christ: The New Testament does not quote Psalm 133, but it takes up its themes. Jesus prayed that his followers would be one, as he and the Father are one, so that the world would believe (John 17:21). Paul urged the church to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Ephesians 4:3). The early church in Jerusalem, gathered in one place, experienced the Spirit poured out on them (Acts 2:1-4), and afterward they held all things in common and were of one heart and soul (Acts 4:32). Christian interpreters have also noted that Jesus is the Anointed One, the Christ, and that believers share in his anointing through the Spirit (1 John 2:20, 27), which some connect with the oil that runs down from Aaron's head to his whole body. That connection is thematic, not predictive.
questions: The psalm calls unity good and pleasant. Where have you experienced that kind of unity, and what made it possible?
The oil and the dew both come down from above. What does that suggest about where unity among God's people comes from?
What divisions in your family, church, or community most need the kind of blessing this psalm describes? What might you do to make room for it?
